pos: n. (proper name; a family of the Nethinims who returned from Babylon)
etymology: Hebrew Qeros, of uncertain derivation, perhaps ankle or crooked; the head of a family of Nethinims, named at Ezra 2:44 and Nehemiah 7:47.
biblical_def: Keros is the head of a family of the Nethinims — the given ones, the servants attached to the service of the temple — whose children came back from Babylon with the first company. The register begins: “The Nethinims: the children of Ziha, the children of Hasupha, the children of Tabbaoth” (Ezra 2:43), and continues: “The children of Keros, the children of Siaha, the children of Padon” (Ezra 2:44). Nehemiah gives the same roll a second time, with slight differences of spelling: “The children of Keros, the children of Sia, the children of Padon” (Nehemiah 7:47). The total is small: “All the Nethinims, and the children of Solomon's servants, were three hundred ninety and two” (Ezra 2:58). Three hundred ninety-two men out of a nation, holding the lowest offices of the sanctuary, and God wrote their family names down twice in His book. They had no land, no priesthood and no royal descent. They had the water and the wood of the house of God, and their names in Scripture.

corruption_summary: Worth is reckoned by station; the lowest servants of the temple are registered by family name, twice.
corruption_paragraphs: A man's standing in the ancient world was his descent, and the Nethinims had none worth naming — they were the given ones, temple servants of foreign stock. Scripture records their family names in Ezra and again in Nehemiah, with the same care it gives to the priestly houses. God's registers are not arranged by rank.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God knows and names those who do the lowest work in His house, and that a returning remnant counted its servants as carefully as its priests.

pos: n. (proper name; head of a family among the children of Solomon's servants)
etymology: Hebrew Sotay, of uncertain derivation, perhaps turning aside, from sut, to swerve; named at Ezra 2:55 and Nehemiah 7:57.
biblical_def: Sotai heads the list of the children of Solomon's servants in both of the great registers of the return: “The children of Solomon's servants: the children of Sotai, the children of Sophereth, the children of Peruda” (Ezra 2:55), and “The children of Solomon's servants: the children of Sotai, the children of Sophereth, the children of Perida” (Nehemiah 7:57). Solomon's servants were a class formed when he levied bondmen for the building of the temple and the royal works, and their descendants were still a recognized order five centuries later, still bound to the service of the house of God. The register closes with a count: “All the Nethinims, and the children of Solomon's servants, were three hundred ninety and two” (Ezra 2:58), repeated in Nehemiah: “All the Nethinims, and the children of Solomon's servants, were three hundred ninety and two” (Nehemiah 7:60). Every one of those men had the chance to stay in Babylon, where a servant of the temple would be nobody at all and might make something of himself. They came back to be servants of the temple.

corruption_paragraphs: Exile had loosened the old orders, and a temple bondman's son in Babylon had no particular reason to resume his father's station. Three hundred ninety-two of them went home to do exactly that. They preferred the lowest place in the house of God to an open field in a foreign city.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a place in God's house, however low, is better than liberty away from it, and that a family may inherit a service and keep it gladly.

pos: n. (proper name; head of a family among the children of Solomon's servants)
etymology: Hebrew Sophereth, from sopher, a scribe or writer; the name may mark the family's ancient employment as scribes.
biblical_def: Sophereth is the head of a family among the children of Solomon's servants, named in both registers of the return: “The children of Solomon's servants: the children of Sotai, the children of Sophereth, the children of Peruda” (Ezra 2:55), and “The children of Solomon's servants: the children of Sotai, the children of Sophereth, the children of Perida” (Nehemiah 7:57). The name comes from the Hebrew word for a scribe, and several of the names in these lists appear to be trade names carried down a family — the next verses include “the children of Pochereth of Zebaim” (Ezra 2:57), a name connected with the catching of game. Both registers end with the same figure: “All the Nethinims, and the children of Solomon's servants, were three hundred ninety and two” (Ezra 2:58), and “All the Nethinims, and the children of Solomon's servants, were three hundred ninety and two” (Nehemiah 7:60). That two independent registers, drawn up a century apart, agree to the man is no small testimony to the care with which Israel kept its books and the Holy Ghost preserved them.

corruption_summary: Scripture's lists are called careless; two registers a century apart agree to the man on the count of the temple servants.
corruption_paragraphs: The genealogies of Ezra and Nehemiah are often cited for their small differences of spelling, as though the whole were loose. Set beside those differences is the agreement: both registers close the Nethinims and Solomon's servants at three hundred ninety and two. Varying forms of a name and an exact agreement in the sum are the marks of real records, not invented ones.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the reliability of the inspired registers, and the honour of an ordinary family trade carried through generations into the service of God's house.

pos: n. (proper name; head of a family of Solomon's servants, also written Peruda)
etymology: Hebrew Perida, perhaps separation, from parad, to divide or separate; written Peruda in Ezra and Perida in Nehemiah.
biblical_def: Perida is the head of a family among the children of Solomon's servants. Nehemiah's register gives his name in this form: “The children of Solomon's servants: the children of Sotai, the children of Sophereth, the children of Perida” (Nehemiah 7:57); Ezra's gives it as Peruda: “The children of Solomon's servants: the children of Sotai, the children of Sophereth, the children of Peruda” (Ezra 2:55), and the margin of the Authorized Version notes the two as one. The same family, the same place in the order, two spellings of one Hebrew name. The lists close with an identical count in both books: “All the Nethinims, and the children of Solomon's servants, were three hundred ninety and two” (Ezra 2:58), and “All the Nethinims, and the children of Solomon's servants, were three hundred ninety and two” (Nehemiah 7:60). His name probably means separation, and separation is what the whole return was about — a people cut off from the land of their captivity and brought back to serve in the house of their God.

corruption_paragraphs: Two books of the Bible spell this family's name differently, which is offered as evidence of carelessness in the text. The name stands at the identical point in an identically ordered list, between Sophereth and the next house, and both registers end at the same total. Hebrew names were written in more than one way; that is a fact about Hebrew, not a fault in Scripture.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the inspired registers are trustworthy on their own terms, and that separation from the world unto the service of God is the pattern of the whole return.

pos: n. (proper name; a family of the Nethinims, also written Sia)
etymology: Hebrew Si'aha, of uncertain derivation; written Sia in Nehemiah's register, and noted as one name in the margin of the Authorized Version.
biblical_def: Siaha heads a family of the Nethinims who returned from Babylon: “The children of Keros, the children of Siaha, the children of Padon” (Ezra 2:44). Nehemiah's register gives the name in the shorter form: “The children of Keros, the children of Sia, the children of Padon” (Nehemiah 7:47), and the margin of the Authorized Version notes the two as one. The list begins the same way in both books: “The Nethinims: the children of Ziha, the children of Hashupha, the children of Tabbaoth” (Nehemiah 7:46). These were the temple servants, and they were few: “All the Nethinims, and the children of Solomon's servants, were three hundred ninety and two” (Ezra 2:58). Many of the Nethinim names are not Hebrew at all, which fits what we know of their origin — they were given to the service of the sanctuary out of conquered peoples, as the Gibeonites were given to be hewers of wood and drawers of water. Foreigners by blood, they are named in the holy register, and their sons came home from Babylon to the work their fathers had done.

pos: n. (proper name; one of the sons of Nebo who put away a strange wife under Ezra)
etymology: Hebrew Zebina, perhaps purchased or bought, from a root signifying to buy; named once, at Ezra 10:43.
biblical_def: Zebina is one of the men who had married a foreign wife and gave her up when Ezra called the nation to account: “Of the sons of Nebo; Jeiel, Mattithiah, Zabad, Zebina, Jadau, and Joel, Benaiah” (Ezra 10:43). The demand had been put to the whole congregation without softening: “Now therefore make confession unto the LORD God of your fathers, and do his pleasure: and separate yourselves from the people of the land, and from the strange wives” (Ezra 10:11), and the congregation agreed aloud: “Then all the congregation answered and said with a loud voice, As thou hast said, so must we do” (Ezra 10:12). The chapter then names the men — priests, Levites, singers, porters and people — family by family, and ends with the hardest line in the book: “All these had taken strange wives: and some of them had wives by whom they had children” (Ezra 10:44). There is no attempt to make this easy reading. Men who had done a thing God forbade, and who had built households on it, were brought to confess it by name, in a list, in Scripture. Zebina is on that list.

corruption_summary: Repentance is expected to be private and costless; Ezra's offenders are named one by one and the cost is stated.
corruption_paragraphs: We prefer repentance that is general, unnamed and leaves the arrangements of our lives untouched. Ezra ten is a list of names, house by house, of men who confessed a specific sin and paid for it in their own households. The chapter does not minimize what it cost, and it does not excuse the sin because it had cost something to undo.
This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that true repentance is particular, public where the sin was public, and willing to dismantle what sin has built.

pos: n. (proper name; a man of Judah who dwelt in Jerusalem, and a returning exile under Ezra)
etymology: Hebrew Uthay, of uncertain derivation, perhaps my helper or helpful; named at 1 Chronicles 9:4 and Ezra 8:14.
biblical_def: Uthai is named twice in Scripture, and both times in connection with the repopulating of Jerusalem after the captivity. The Chronicler lists him first among the men of Judah who settled in the city: “And in Jerusalem dwelt of the children of Judah, and of the children of Benjamin, and of the children of Ephraim, and Manasseh” (1 Chronicles 9:3), and then “Uthai the son of Ammihud, the son of Omri, the son of Imri, the son of Bani, of the children of Pharez the son of Judah” (1 Chronicles 9:4) — four generations given, to establish his right to the city. The other mention is in Ezra's muster of those who came up with him from Babylon: “Of the sons also of Bigvai; Uthai, and Zabbud, and with them seventy males” (Ezra 8:14). That company gathered at a river and found a lack: “And I gathered them together to the river that runneth to Ahava; and there abode we in tents three days: and I viewed the people, and the priests, and found there none of the sons of Levi” (Ezra 8:15). Ezra would not set out until Levites were found and the company had fasted and sought God for the road.

corruption_summary: Resettling a ruined city is thought a matter of logistics; the Chronicler records four generations to show whose right it was to dwell there.
corruption_paragraphs: Jerusalem after the exile was a half-empty ruin, and one might expect that anyone willing to live in it would be welcome on any terms. The record is more careful than that. Uthai's descent is traced four generations back to Pharez the son of Judah, because the city and its land belonged to families by God's own allotment, and the restoration had to be a restoration of the right people to the right place.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God's people are restored according to His order and not merely according to willingness, and that a man who will not move without God's appointed ministers, as Ezra would not, is wise.

pos: n. (proper name; a son of Bebai under Ezra, and the father of Baruch who repaired the wall)
etymology: Hebrew Zabbay, perhaps pure or a shortened form of Zebadiah, the LORD has given; the AV margin at Nehemiah 3:20 notes the reading Zaccai.
biblical_def: Zabbai is named twice. The first time he is among the men who had married strange wives and were brought to confession under Ezra: “Of the sons also of Bebai; Jehohanan, Hananiah, Zabbai, and Athlai” (Ezra 10:28), the whole proceeding having opened with Ezra's charge: “Now therefore make confession unto the LORD God of your fathers, and do his pleasure: and separate yourselves from the people of the land, and from the strange wives” (Ezra 10:11). The second time, his son is at work on the wall: “After him Baruch the son of Zabbai earnestly repaired the other piece, from the turning of the wall unto the door of the house of Eliashib the high priest” (Nehemiah 3:20). The word earnestly is used of no other builder in the chapter; of the next man it says simply, “After him repaired Meremoth the son of Urijah the son of Koz another piece, from the door of the house of Eliashib even to the end of the house of Eliashib” (Nehemiah 3:21). If these are the same family, then a father who had to confess a sin raised a son whom the Holy Ghost singles out for the zeal of his work on Jerusalem's wall.

pos: n. (proper name; father of one of the heads of families who returned with Ezra)
etymology: Hebrew Yosiphyah, the LORD will add, from yasaph, to add, with the divine name — the same root as in Joseph.
biblical_def: Josiphiah is named once, in the muster roll of the men who went up with Ezra from Babylon: “And of the sons of Shelomith; the son of Josiphiah, and with him an hundred and threescore males” (Ezra 8:10). The roll is introduced as a genealogy: “These are now the chief of their fathers, and this is the genealogy of them that went up with me from Babylon, in the reign of Artaxerxes the king” (Ezra 8:1). Before that company moved, Ezra did two things worth remembering. He refused to ask the king for an escort, and instead called a fast: “Then I proclaimed a fast there, at the river of Ahava, that we might afflict ourselves before our God, to seek of him a right way for us, and for our little ones, and for all our substance” (Ezra 8:21). And the journey was made and the outcome recorded: “Then we departed from the river of Ahava on the twelfth day of the first month, to go unto Jerusalem: and the hand of our God was upon us, and he delivered us from the hand of the enemy, and of such as lay in wait by the way” (Ezra 8:31). The name means the LORD will add, and a hundred and sixty males went up under his son.

corruption_summary: Prudence is set against faith; Ezra would not ask the king for soldiers, and fasted at the river instead.
corruption_paragraphs: Ezra was ashamed to request a band of horsemen from Artaxerxes, having told the king that the hand of God was upon all who seek Him. So he fasted with the whole company, little ones and substance included, and went four months' road without escort. He is explicit about the result: the hand of our God was upon us, and he delivered us. That is not recklessness; it is a man refusing to contradict his own testimony.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that seeking a right way of God by fasting and prayer is the first provision for a journey, and that His keeping is to be published when it comes.

pos: n. (proper name; one of the sons of Bani who put away a strange wife under Ezra)
etymology: Hebrew Ma'aday, perhaps ornament of the LORD, from adah, to adorn; named once, at Ezra 10:34.
biblical_def: Maadai is one of the sons of Bani named in Ezra's register of the men who had taken foreign wives: “Of the sons of Bani; Maadai, Amram, and Uel” (Ezra 10:34), and the list runs straight on: “Benaiah, Bedeiah, Chelluh” (Ezra 10:35). The sons of Hashum had been named in the verse before: “Of the sons of Hashum; Mattenai, Mattathah, Zabad, Eliphelet, Jeremai, Manasseh, and Shimei” (Ezra 10:33). House after house, the men are set down by name. The chapter will not let the matter be general. And it ends with the sentence that gives the whole affair its weight: “All these had taken strange wives: and some of them had wives by whom they had children” (Ezra 10:44). The family of Bani was among the heaviest offenders in the record, which is why the list under their name is so long. Scripture names them anyway. A register of the repentant is also a register of the guilty, and God was willing for both to be read together in His book.

corruption_summary: Church records are kept to flatter; Ezra's register names the guilty and the repentant in the same breath.
corruption_paragraphs: No institution writes down the names of its own offenders if it can help it. Ezra ten does nothing else for most of its length: house after house, man after man, each one named as having taken a strange wife, and the family of Bani filling more lines than any other. The same list is their confession.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God is honoured by honest records, that a congregation may face a widespread sin by name without being destroyed by it, and that confession is the beginning of restoration.
